newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta to squirm as Spain puts rate cuts on hold.
newsitem.headline: Peseta to squirm as Spain puts rate cuts on hold.

text.p: Pressure on the peseta to appreciate is gathering steam as the Bank of Spain shies away from cutting interest rates amid signs of a rebounding economy, analysts said on Friday.

With Spanish interest rates still way above German rates, and the Bank of Spain making signs that it is unlikely to cut rates soon, the peseta could make a dash for the key 84.00 per mark level this summer, analysts said.

For many months, the peseta has remained at the mercy of the central bank which has intervened heavily to stabilise the currency in the 84.00 to 85.00 per mark band in the run up to a single European currency.
Economists said signs that currency reserves were beginning to grow was evidence that the central bank was already having to stave off peseta strength which has slowly been bubbling up.
"They have been buying (marks) -- currency reserves rose two percent in May and June," said Francesco Giordano, economist at CSFB in London.
A string of buoyant data in recent weeks has provided mounting evidence that Spain's monetary easing cycle will be put on the back-burner until at least after the summer.

While Spain has reduced its key interest rate 12 times since December 1995, slashing it from 9.25 percent to a current level of 5.25 percent, it is still a way off from Germany's repo rate at 3.0 percent.

"Given that analysts believe the peseta will likely enter European economic and monetary union (EMU) at a central parity of around 85.07, the interest rate differential to Germany implies a stronger currency than at present," said one analyst.
On Friday, the peseta was trading around 84.40 per mark.
Some analysts agreed that the peseta would soon face upward pressure, but instead insisted that it would be a result of a rebound in the debt markets towards the end of the summer.

"At the end of August we will have the first news on the budget which is likely to be tight and this will cheer debt markets bringing investors back and putting upward pressure on the peseta," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
However, he doubted the currency would break through 84.00 per mark, with inflation under control and Spain competitive versus the rest of Europe.
Some analysts said the onset of the tourist season would give the peseta an added push. Spain is the world's number two tourist destination in terms of receipts after the United States.
"The peseta is always slightly stronger in the summer due to demand for tourist receipts," one analyst said.
Spain said it expected a record number of tourists to visit in 1997. A record 41.2 million tourists visited Spain in 1996, generating an income of 3.5 billion pesetas.
